default.q.n3-12-q31-31.why.2: Incorrect because 「健康」 is not used to describe the sound, durable condition of a building or structure; 「丈夫」 or 「頑丈」 should be used for buildings.
default.q.n3-12-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect because 「健康」 is not used for machines or electronic devices. For a computer that is not functioning normally, use 「調子が良くない」.
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is 1 because 「参加」combines correctly with nouns referring to events and seminars (「セミナーに参加する」—to participate in a seminar).
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.explanation:
「参加」（さんか）is a noun and a Group 3 verb meaning "to participate" or "to take part," used when someone joins or attends an activity, event, organization, seminar, or competition (such as セミナー・会議・イベント・ツアー・試合に参加する).
Example: 来週のボランティア活動に参加する予定です。(I plan to participate in next week’s volunteer activity.)
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.why.0: Correct. 「参加」 naturally combines with nouns referring to events or seminars, as in 「留学セミナーに参加する」 (“participate in a study-abroad seminar”).
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect because entering or going into a forest takes 「入る」 (はいる) or 「行く」, not 「参加する」.
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect because being caught in a traffic jam is expressed as 「渋滞に巻き込まれる」 or 「渋滞にはまる」, not 「参加する」.
default.q.n3-12-q32-32.why.3: This is incorrect. When a new member joins a family, use 「加わる」(くわわる) or 「仲間入りする」, not 「参加する」.
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 3 because 「中旬」 correctly refers to the middle part of a month, from the 11th through the 20th.
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.explanation:
「中旬」（ちゅうじゅん）means “the middle of the month” (approximately the 11th through the 20th). In Japanese, a month is divided into three periods: 上旬 (じょうじゅん: the 1st–10th), 中旬 (ちゅうじゅん: the 11th–20th), and 下旬 (げじゅん: the 21st–end of the month). This word is used only for time within a month, not for spatial position, the progress of a match, or birth order among siblings.
Example: 桜は4月中旬に見頃を迎えます。(The cherry blossoms are at their best around the middle of April.)
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.why.0: Incorrect because 「中旬」 refers to the middle period of a month, not the position of a bookshelf compartment or shelf. For a middle position, use 「真ん中」 or 「中段」.
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.why.1: Incorrect because the middle of a sports match is expressed with 「途中」 or 「中盤」(ちゅうばん), not 「中旬」.
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.why.2: Correct because 「中旬」 refers to the period from the 11th to the 20th of a month (「来月の中旬」—the middle of next month).
default.q.n3-12-q33-33.why.3: This is incorrect. For the child in the middle or the second-born among siblings, use 「真ん中」, not 「中旬」, which refers to the middle of a month.
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 3 because 「落ち着く」correctly combines with a feeling or state of mind, as in 「気持ちが落ち着く」(to feel calm and relaxed).
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.explanation:
「落ち着く」（おちつく）is an intransitive verb meaning "to calm down" or "to become composed" when referring to one's feelings; "to settle down" or "to stabilize" when referring to a situation or lifestyle; or "to be calm and tasteful" when referring to a space or color. Common expressions include: 気持ち／心が落ち着く, 生活が落ち着く, 落ち着いた雰囲気.
Example: 深呼吸をしたら、少し気持ちが落ち着いてきた。(After taking a deep breath, I began to feel a little calmer.)
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.why.0: Incorrect because when many people are standing in line or gathered in front of a shop, 「並んでいる」or「集まっている」is used, not「落ち着いている」.
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.why.1: Incorrect: for an object lying or placed on the floor, use 「置いてある」 or 「転がっている」, not 「落ち着いている」.
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.why.2: Correct because the phrase「気持ちが落ち着く」accurately describes feeling calm and relaxed while listening to a favorite piece of music.
default.q.n3-12-q34-34.why.3: Incorrect because for scattered or strewn rubbish on the road, use 「落ちている」or「散らかっている」, not 「落ち着いている」.
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is sentence 2 because 「ほえる」(吠える) correctly refers to a dog's bark (「犬がほえる」).
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.explanation:
「ほえる」（吠える／吼える）is a verb meaning “bark” when used for dogs: 犬が吠える, or “roar” or “howl” when used for wild animals such as tigers, lions, and wolves. For birds singing or cats meowing, use 「鳴く」（なく）; for bells or music ringing or playing, use 「鳴る」（なる）or 「流れる」.
Example: 見知らぬ人が近づくと、番犬が激しくほえた。(When a stranger approached, the guard dog barked fiercely.)
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.why.0: Incorrect because bird songs use the verbs 「鳴く」(なく) or 「さえずる」, not 「ほえる」.
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.why.1: Correct because 「ほえる」（吠える）is exactly the right verb for describing a dog barking (「犬がほえている」: the dog is barking).
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.why.2: Incorrect because when an alarm clock rings, the verb 「鳴る」 (なる) is used, not 「ほえる」.
default.q.n3-12-q35-35.why.3: Incorrect because music playing or sounding in a store is expressed with 「流れている」or「鳴っている」, not 「ほえる」.
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 2. も, because the structure 「何時間も」 emphasizes that the period lasts for many consecutive hours.
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.explanation:
Sentence meaning: When I ran into a friend from high school, I was so happy that I ended up talking for several hours.
- Grammar:「Number/何 + counter + も」emphasizes a large quantity (here, 何時間も = for many hours / several hours straight).
- Example: コンサートには何万人もの人が集まった。(Tens of thousands of people gathered at the concert.)
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.why.0: (a) 「は」marks the topic or a minimum degree, and does not convey emphasis on a large quantity.
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.why.1: (b) 「も」 is correct; after a quantity expression (何時間も), it emphasizes a longer-than-expected period of time ("for several hours").
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.why.2: (c) 「が」 is the particle marking the subject and cannot directly follow a time quantity to modify the verb 話す in this way.
default.q.n3-13-q36-36.why.3: (d) 「を」marks a direct object or a route/distance traveled; it does not directly follow 何時間 to modify the verb 話す.
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.verdict: The correct answer is 4. を is used because the structure「〜を中心に」means “centered on...” or “mainly directed toward...”.
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.explanation:
Meaning: This fashion magazine is popular with many people, mainly targeting women aged 20 to 25.
- Kanji meaning: 中心 (center, main focus).
- Grammar: 「N + を中心に / を中心として」= centered on N, mainly involving N.
- Example: この映画は若者を中心に大ヒットしている。(This movie is a huge hit, especially among young people.)
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.why.0: (a) 「に」is incorrect because the standard pattern expressing the central focus is 「〜を中心に」; the particle に is not used here.
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.why.1: (b) 「で」is incorrect because the grammar pattern「〜で中心に」does not exist.
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.why.2: (c) 「は」is incorrect because the particle は does not form a standard grammatical structure before 中心.
default.q.n3-13-q37-37.why.3: (d) 「を」 is correct; it forms the N3 grammar pattern 「N を中心に」 (centered on N).
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.verdict: The correct answer is 4. どうしても, because the adverb「どうしても」often appears with a negative potential form to mean “no matter how hard one tries, one simply cannot...”.
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.explanation:
Meaning: At yesterday's party, I talked a lot with someone I had just met, but I simply cannot remember his name.
- Pattern: 「どうしても + V-ない / V-れない」= no matter how hard one tries, cannot...
- Example: どうしてもその問題の答えが分からない。(I simply cannot figure out the answer to that problem.)
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.why.0: (a) 「必ず」 (“certainly, without fail”) expresses certainty or a command and is used with affirmative sentences, so it does not fit a negative possibility sentence.
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.why.1: (b) 「必ずしも」(not necessarily, not always) commonly occurs with 「〜とは限らない / 〜わけではない」 to express partial negation.
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.why.2: (c) 「どうか」("please") is used in requests and appeals, commonly with ください or お願いします.
default.q.n3-13-q38-38.why.3: (d) 「どうしても」 is correct. Combined with a negative potential verb, it means "no matter how hard one tries": どうしても思い出せない = "cannot remember no matter how hard one tries."
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.verdict: The correct answer is 1. のほかに, because the structure 「〜のほかに」 means “besides ..., there is also ...”.
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.explanation:
Meaning: To apply for a scholarship, you need information such as a transcript in addition to the application form.
- Kanji-derived meanings: 奨学金 (scholarship), 申請 (application), 成績証明書 (academic transcript).
- Grammar:「N + のほかに / V-dictionary・V-ta + ほかに」= in addition to..., besides...
- Example: 英語のほかに、日本語も話せます。(Besides English, I can also speak Japanese.)
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.why.0: (a) 「のほかに」is correct; the pattern 「N + のほかに」 means “in addition to N,” which fits listing additional required documents.
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.why.1: (b) 「のことで」means “about” or “concerning,” and is not used to connect additional nouns in a list.
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.why.2: (c) 「について」 means “about” or “concerning” a topic, so it is unsuitable in the context of additional documents that must be submitted.
default.q.n3-13-q39-39.why.3: (d) 「にくらべて」 means “compared with,” which does not fit because the sentence does not express a comparison.
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 2. うちに because the pattern 「V-ないうちに」 means "while still not ... / before ...".
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.explanation:
Meaning of the dialogue:
A: “Oh, it's starting to rain.”
B: “Oh, you're right. I hear it is going to rain heavily tonight. Let's hurry home before the rain gets heavy.”
- Grammar: 「V-ないうちに」= before... / while it is still not... (doing something before the current state changes).
- Example: 暗くならないうちに、家に帰りましょう。(Let's go home before it gets dark.)
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.why.0: (a) 「ように」 means "so that/in order to," but hurrying home cannot prevent heavy rain from falling, so it does not fit the logic.
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.why.1: (b) 「うちに」is correct; the pattern 「V-ないうちに」means taking action before an undesirable situation occurs ("before it starts raining heavily").
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.why.2: (c) 「ために」 means "in order to/because of" and is not used in the negative form to express making use of time before a change in the weather.
default.q.n3-13-q40-40.why.3: (d) 「までに」usually combines with the dictionary form V-る to indicate a deadline; it does not form「〜ないまでに」.
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.verdict: The correct answer is 1. くださいます because the subject is 社長, a superior, who performs the action of buying a gift for us (〜てくださる is the respectful form of 〜てくれる).
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.explanation:
Meaning: The company president always brings us souvenirs whenever he returns from a business trip.
- Kanji compounds: 社長 (company president), 出張 (business trip), お土産 (souvenir).
- Grammar: 「[superior] は [me/us] に〜てくださいます」 means that [a superior] does something for [me/us]; it is the honorific form of 〜てくれます.
- Example: 先生が本を貸してくださいました。(The teacher lent me a book.)
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.why.0: (a) 「くださいます」 is correct; it is the respectful form of 「〜てくれます」, used when someone senior does something for the speaker or the speaker’s group.
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.why.1: (b) 「いただきます」is the humble form of 「〜てもらいます」, so the subject must be the recipient (we/us); it cannot be used with 「社長は」as the subject.
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.why.2: (c) 「差し上げます」 is the humble form of 「〜てあげます」, used when doing something for another person or someone of higher status.
default.q.n3-13-q41-41.why.3: (d) 「召し上がります」 is the honorific form of 「食べる・飲む」 (to eat/drink) and is not used as a supplementary verb after 「買ってきて」.
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 来ちゃう because 「〜てしまう」 (colloquial: 〜ちゃう) used with 「もうすぐ」 expresses that something is about to happen urgently, and will be missed if one does not hurry.
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.explanation:
Translation:
Younger sister: “Sis, the train is about to arrive!”
Older sister: “I know. Let’s hurry.”
- Grammar: 「〜てしまう / 〜ちゃう」in colloquial speech, used with 「もうすぐ」, expresses an imminent event that is unwanted or creates urgency to act immediately.
- Example: もうすぐバスが出ちゃうから急いで！(The bus is about to leave, so hurry!)
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.why.0: (a) 「来てる」 (“is coming / has arrived”) indicates an ongoing state or arrival, so it does not fit with 「もうすぐ」 when urging someone urgently.
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.why.1: (b) 「来とく」 (a shortened form of 来ておく) means intentionally doing something in advance or preparing it beforehand; a train or other vehicle cannot “prepare itself in advance.”
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.why.2: (c) 「来ちゃう」, a contraction of 来てしまう, is correct; it expresses an imminent event with a sense of urgency (“The train is about to arrive!”).
default.q.n3-13-q42-42.why.3: (d) 「来なきゃ」, abbreviated from 来なければならない, means “must come,” which does not fit the context of urging one’s sister to hurry.
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ないはずがない because the double-negative structure 「〜ないはずがない」 (“there is no way that ... is not,” “it must be”) fits the mother’s basis for judgment: she had just seen the book being used yesterday.
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.explanation:
Meaning:
Child: “Where's my math textbook? It's not here.”
Mother: “Huh? There's no way it isn't here. I saw you doing your homework yesterday. Look again.”
- Sino-Japanese character notes: 算数 (elementary-school mathematics), 教科書 (textbook), 宿題 (homework).
- Double-negative grammar: 「V-ない + はずがない」= “There is no way that … not …” / “It must certainly be …” (a strong assertion based on reliable evidence).
- Example: 一生懸命勉強したのだから、合格できないはずがない。(You studied so hard, so there is no way you won't pass.)
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.why.0: (a) 「ないに違いない」 (“must not exist”) expresses a conclusion completely opposite to the mother's meaning, since she saw her child studying yesterday.
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.why.1: (b) 「ないはずがない」 (“there is no way there is not... / there must certainly be...”) is correct. It expresses a strong assertion based on clear evidence.
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.why.2: (c) 「なくてはいけない」 (“must have, be required to have”) expresses obligation or necessity and is not used to judge whether an object exists.
default.q.n3-13-q43-43.why.3: (d) 「なくてもおかしくない」 means “it would not be strange even if there were none,” indicating that the absence is normal. This contradicts the mother’s explanation in the following sentence.
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.verdict: The correct answer is 1. どちらからでも because 「どちらからでも」means “from either station,” which fits a choice between two stations.
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.explanation:
Meaning: There are Morinaka Station and Minamikawa Station near my university, and I can get to campus from either station. I usually walk from Morinaka Station.
Grammar: 「Question word + でも」 = any/either ... (here, 「どちらからでも」 means from either one of the two stations).
Example: この料理は温かくても冷たくても、どちらでも美味しく召し上がれます。(This dish is delicious whether you eat it hot or cold.)
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.why.0: (a) 「どちらからでも」is correct. 「どちら」(either of two) combines with 「からでも」(from either place) to mean “one can get to school from either station.”
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.why.1: (b) 「どちらかどうか」 expresses uncertainty about which of two possibilities is correct, and cannot function as an adverbial expression of origin before 「大学に行けます」.
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.why.2: (c) 「どっちかも」 is grammatically incorrect, lacks the particle から indicating the starting point, and has an ambiguous meaning.
default.q.n3-13-q44-44.why.3: (d) 「あっちこっちから」 means “from all over the place” and is generally used for multiple mixed locations, not when comparing two specific stations.
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 柔らかくなる, because the subject is marked by the particle 「が」 (キャベツが), so the intransitive form expressing a change of state, 「〜くなる」, is required.
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.explanation:
Meaning:
Teacher: "When the water boils, add the salt and cabbage to the hot water, then wait until the cabbage becomes tender."
- Kanji readings: 沸騰 ( - boil), 柔らかい ( - soft).
- Change-of-state grammar: Remove い from an -い adjective and add くなる. This expresses a spontaneous change of state and is used with the particle が.
- Example: 寒くなってきたので、コートを着ました。(It started getting cold, so I put on a coat.)
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.why.0: (a) 「柔らかくする」is a transitive verb meaning “to make soft,” and takes the particle を (キャベツを柔らかくする), not が.
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.why.1: (b) 「柔らかくにる」is grammatically incorrect because an i-adjective does not conjugate into「〜くにる」.
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.why.2: (c) 「柔らかくなる」 is correct; 「A(い) remove い + くなる」 expresses a natural change of state in the subject marked by が (the cabbage becomes soft).
default.q.n3-13-q45-45.why.3: (d) 「柔らかく」 is an adverbial form, so it must be followed by a complete dictionary-form verb (V-る) before まで.
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.verdict: The correct answer is 2. のに because it expresses a contrast: “Even though I followed the recipe correctly, it still failed.”
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.explanation:
Meaning: Yesterday, I tried making bread for the first time. I followed the recipe I found online exactly, but I still failed.
- Kanji vocabulary: 失敗 (failure, fail).
- Grammar:「V・A・N (plain form) + のに」= even though, despite the fact that (expresses a result contrary to expectations or predictions).
- Example: 薬を飲んだのに、熱が下がりません。(Even though I took medicine, my fever still hasn't gone down.)
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.why.0: (a) 「から」indicates a straightforward cause-and-effect relationship (“because..., therefore...”); it does not fit the logic of failing despite following the formula correctly.
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.why.1: (b) 「のに」 is correct; the pattern 「V-plain form + のに」 expresses an unexpected result along with a sense of regret (“even though,” “and yet”).
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.why.2: (c) 「のは」 nominalizes a clause to make it the subject; it is not used to connect two contrastive clauses.
default.q.n3-13-q46-46.why.3: (d) 「ので」 indicates a favorable objective cause (“because…, therefore…”); it is not used to connect two clauses that contradict each other.
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 入っていたことがあるんだ because the pattern 「〜ていたことがある」is used to share past experiences, such as having once participated in a club.
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.explanation:
Meaning:
Tanaka: "I just started playing tennis. Do you know how to play, Yamashita?"
Yamashita: "Oh, I used to belong to the tennis club at school."
- Grammar: 「V-たことがある / V-ていたことがある」= to have done something before; used to describe past experiences.
- Example: 日本の会社で働いていたことがあります。(I once worked for a Japanese company.)
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.why.0: (a) 「入ったままなんだ」 (remain in the state of having entered) expresses an unchanged state after an action, so it is unsuitable for describing a completed past experience.
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.why.1: (b) 「入ってばかりだったんだ」 (“was only entering”) describes repeated frequency of an action and is meaningless when referring to joining a club.
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.why.2: (c) 「入っていたことがあるんだ」 is correct; the past progressive combined with 「ことがある」 describes the experience of having belonged to the tennis club for a period in the past.
default.q.n3-13-q47-47.why.3: (d)「入っているところだったんだ」(“was just in the process of entering”) indicates an action in progress at a particular time, so it cannot express a past experience.
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.verdict: The correct answer is 2. やすい because the structure 「V-stem + やすい」(使いやすい = easy to use) fits the reason that the dictionary contains many example sentences.
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.explanation:
Meaning:
A: “There are so many kinds of Japanese dictionaries. I cannot decide which one to buy.”
B: “How about this one? Compared with the others, it has many example sentences, and I think it is very easy to use.”
- Kanji note: 辞書 (dictionary), 例文 (example sentence), 比べる (to compare).
- Grammar: 「V-ます (remove ます) + やすい」= easy to do, describing an object that is convenient or easy to handle.
- Example: このペンはとても書きやすいです。(This pen is very easy to write with.)
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.why.0: (a)「すぎる」in「使いすぎる」means “to use too much” or “to overuse,” so it is inappropriate when praising a dictionary’s advantages.
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.why.1: (b)「やすい」is correct; combined with the verb stem after removing -ます (使いやすい), it means “easy to use” and describes the dictionary’s convenient feature.
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.why.2: (c) 「てもいい」is grammatically incorrect because it cannot directly follow the verb stem「使い」. The correct form is 使ってもいい.
default.q.n3-13-q48-48.why.3: (d) When 「そうだ」 forms 「使いそうだ」, it means “looks likely to be used,” which is illogical when evaluating a product’s quality.
default.q.n3-13-q49-49.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (the correct order is: 2 → 4 → 1 → 3; the star ★ marks answer choice 1).
default.q.n3-13-q49-49.explanation:
Complete sentence: X 学校と Y 学校のバスケットボールの試合は 10 時開始の予定だったが、大雨による電車の遅れのため 1 時開始になった。

Because the author only attended Japanese-language classes, there were no opportunities to talk with Japanese students, and the author wondered how to make friends. To express a question about how to accomplish something in the past ('how could I ...?'), the indirect-question pattern 「どうしたら～できるのか」 is combined with the past form 「わかりませんでした」. Therefore, choice 4 is the most accurate.
default.q.n3-13-q54-54.why.0: (a) Answer choice 1 is incorrect because 「知りたいです」 is in the present tense (“I want to know”) and uses direct conversational language, which does not suit a narrative passage recounting past feelings and thoughts.

default.q.n3-13-q54-54.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the past tense in「できたのか」does not fit the pattern asking how to accomplish something,「どうしたら～できるか」(how one can make friends).
default.q.n3-13-q54-54.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the indirect question structure 「どうしたら～できるのか」 (how one can...) combined with the past ending 「わかりませんでした」 accurately expresses the author's confusion and inability to know what to do during the first two months.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 2. そして.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.explanation: Before the blank, the author recounts seeing some students playing basketball in the gym and watching them for a while because the author also liked basketball (「しばらく見ていました」). Then a natural thought arose: joining the club might make it possible to make Japanese friends (「クラブに入れば日本人の友達ができるのではないかと考えました」). These two clauses develop naturally through the sequence of events and thoughts, so the sequential conjunction 「そして」(and then / after that) is the most appropriate choice.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because 「つまり」(in other words; to sum up) summarizes or explains the preceding idea as a definition; it does not connect two actions or thoughts occurring one after another.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because 「そして」(and then / after that) is used as a conjunction to connect a sequence of actions and thoughts in a logical chronological order: after watching for a while, the speaker then has a thought.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because 「ところが」 (“but,” “however”) is used when what follows is completely contrary to or unexpected from the preceding prediction. It does not fit this context.
default.q.n3-13-q55-55.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because 「たとえば」(for example) introduces an example illustrating a preceding statement, which does not fit the flow of the passage.
default.q.n3-13-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ないかもしれないと思いました.
default.q.n3-13-q56-56.explanation: Before the blank, the author says that they were very worried about their Japanese ability and could not bring themselves to ask a question (「なかなか聞けませんでした」). The conjunction 「でも」 (but) then marks a change in direction: if they did not join a club, they might never have a chance to make friends with Japanese students (「クラブに入らなかったら、ずっと...機会はないかもしれないと思いました」). This thought prompted the author to act immediately afterward: 「私は近くにいた学生に話しかけてみました」 (I tried talking to a student who was nearby). Therefore, choice 4 fits perfectly in both grammar and context.
default.q.n3-13-q56-56.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because 「～そうです」(I hear that...) is used to relay information heard from another source, not the author’s inner thoughts.

default.q.n3-13-q56-56.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the ending 「～からです」 (“it is because...”) explains the reason for a result stated earlier, whereas this sentence begins with the contrasting conjunction 「でも」 to shift the line of thought rather than explain the preceding sentence.
default.q.n3-13-q56-56.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the structure 「～かもしれないと思いました」 (“I thought that perhaps...”) accurately expresses a past speculation and inner thought, which motivated the author to overcome their shyness and start a conversation.
default.q.n3-13-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 答えてくれました.
default.q.n3-13-q57-57.explanation: The subject is 「彼女」(the female student), and the action is answering the author’s question attentively (「質問に丁寧に...」). default.q.n3-13-q64-64.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the passage contains no information that the section manager's work has recently become less busy than before.
default.q.n3-13-q64-64.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct, as directly stated in the reading: 「課長は、最近、朝から晩まで仕事のことばかり考えている自分に気づき、これではよくないと考えて、何か新しいことをやってみたいと思ったそうです。」 (The section chief realized that recently he had been thinking about work from morning until night, decided that this was not good, and wanted to try something new.)
default.q.n3-13-q64-64.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because feeling that work has become smoother is the result after taking piano lessons (「前より仕事もうまくいくようになった気がするんだよ」), not the original thought or reason that prompted the man to begin.
default.q.n3-13-q64-64.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because 「子供のころ習いたかったこと」 refers to something the department manager wanted to learn when he or she was a child, not something the manager wanted to start learning together with their own child.
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is 1: I also plan to look for a ballet class.
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.explanation:
Summary: After hearing the department manager's story about taking piano lessons to fulfill a childhood dream, the speaker is also inspired and plans to look for ballet lessons, which they have wanted to take since childhood.

Question translation: Which option is the most appropriate for filling in the blank （　）?
Answer choices:
1. Look for ballet lessons
2. Finish the work early
3. Look for piano lessons
4. Look for something they want to do
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is correct, as shown by the passage: 「課長の話を聞いて、私も何かやりたくなりました。実は、子供のころからバレエを習いたいと思っていたので、私も（バレエ教室を探す）つもりです。」 Just as the section chief found a nearby piano class to fulfill a childhood wish, the narrator has wanted to learn ballet since childhood and therefore plans to look for a ballet class as well.
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because the speaker's purpose is to learn a new skill or hobby, not to finish work early.
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the speaker wants to learn ballet (「バレエを習いたい」), not piano (「ピアノ」).
default.q.n3-13-q65-65.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the speaker had already clearly decided from childhood that they wanted to learn ballet (「実は、子供のころからバレエを習いたいと思っていた」), rather than searching for something else they might want to do.
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 大学に合格してほしいという気持ち (the wish for the examinee to pass the university entrance exam).
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.explanation:
- Main idea: When a bank teller gave the narrator a pentagonal pencil, the teller explained that 五角 (gokaku, pentagon) sounds similar to 合格 (goukaku, pass an exam), so the pencil was given to the examinee as a wish for them to pass.
- Question translation: What sentiment did the bank teller want to convey by giving “me” the pencil?
- Answer choices:
  1. The wish that I would study hard after entering university
  2. The wish that I would take an entrance exam for a Japanese university
  3. The wish that I would pass the university entrance exam
  4. Congratulations on passing the university entrance exam
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the staff member gave the pencil to encourage the candidate to pass the upcoming university entrance examination, not to talk about working hard after entering university.
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author was already in Japan and went to the bank to pay the examination fee. The staff member was not encouraging the author to take the exam but wishing them success.
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.why.2: (c) Correct, because the bank employee clearly explains: 「『五角(ごかく)』 と『合格(ごうかく)』は発音が似ているから、合格を願って、受験生にお渡ししているんです。」 (Because "pentagon" and "passing an exam" sound alike, we give them to examinees as a wish for their success).
default.q.n3-13-q66-66.why.3: (d) Incorrect. At this point, the writer has only paid the examination fee and is preparing to take the exam; they have not passed yet, so this is not a congratulatory message for entering university.
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is 3: 日本の銀行が、言葉遊びを使って面白いサービスをしていること (The fact that Japanese banks use wordplay to offer interesting services).
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.explanation:
- Main point: The author was not surprised by the homophone wordplay itself, since the author's own country has it too. Rather, the author was surprised that in Japan, a solemn place such as a bank used this amusing wordplay as a gift-giving service to encourage customers.
- Question translation: The passage says that the author was "slightly surprised." What surprised the author?
- Answer choices:
  1. The fact that the Japanese pronunciations of "pentagon" and "passing an exam" are the same.
  2. The fact that Japan also has wordplay using words with the same pronunciation but different meanings.
  3. The fact that a bank in Japan used wordplay to provide an entertaining service.
  4. The fact that the service of a Japanese bank was similar to that of a bank in the author's country.
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author’s surprise is not limited to the existence of homophones in Japanese; it lies in the bank using them as a gift service.
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author says that their own country also has similar wordplay (「私の国にも...言葉遊びもある」); what is surprising is that a bank in Japan launched this activity.
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.why.2: (c) Correct because the author clearly states the surprising reason: 「でも、日本では銀行でこのようなサービスをしているのだ。（と思った）」 (But in Japan, even banks provide this kind of service).
default.q.n3-13-q67-67.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author was surprised by the uniqueness of the service at the Japanese bank and did not compare it with a similar service in their home country.
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 2: 実際の効果があってもなくても、応援してもらった人は喜ぶだろう。 (Whether it actually has an effect or not, the person being supported will probably be happy).
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.explanation:
- Main idea: Regarding this kind of encouragement, the author thinks that although it is not known whether it will actually help someone pass, what matters most is the sincerity behind it; anyone who receives such encouragement while making an effort will feel happy.
- Question translation: What does “I” think about this kind of encouragement?
- Answer choices:
  1. Because it is effective in reality, the person being encouraged will certainly be happy.
  2. Whether or not it is effective in reality, the person being encouraged will certainly be happy.
  3. Because it is unclear whether it is effective in reality, it would be better if the encouragement were more effective.
  4. Because it is ineffective in reality, only the person giving the encouragement feels happy.
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author writes 「実際に効果があるかどうかわからない」 (“I do not know whether it is actually effective”), rather than confidently asserting that it is effective.
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.why.1: (b) Correct because the final sentence states: 「このような応援は、実際に効果があるかどうかわからない。しかし、大切なのは気持ちだ。自分が頑張っているときに、こうやって応援してもらったら、誰でもうれしいだろう。」 Whether or not the encouragement is effective, the recipient will still feel happy because of the thought behind it.
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the author emphasizes that one’s feelings are what matter, not that a more effective way of cheering is needed.
default.q.n3-13-q68-68.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author does not claim that it is “ineffective,” and says that anyone who receives encouragement will be happy («誰でもうれしいだろう»), not only the person giving the encouragement.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 4: A lifestyle that keeps and owns only things that are truly necessary and appealing.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.explanation:
Paragraph 1 explains the concept of "a life without possessions" (持たない生活): reducing one's belongings as much as possible and keeping only the things one truly needs and likes, so that everyday life remains comfortable and pleasant.

Question translation:
"What kind of life is a 'life without possessions'?"

Answer choices:
1. A life surrounded only by items featured in magazines.
2. A life of denying oneself purchases even when there is something one wants.
3. A life that reduces even necessary and beloved possessions as much as possible.
4. A life that tries to own only the things that are necessary and beloved.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage only mentions that the author read an introductory article in a magazine, not that the author was surrounded by objects like those shown in the magazine.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage does not mention having to restrain oneself from buying something one wants.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage clearly says to keep necessary and favorite belongings, not to reduce even those items.
default.q.n3-13-q69-69.why.3: (d) Correct because the second sentence of paragraph 1 states: 「物をできるだけ減らして、自分にとって本当に必要で気に入っている物だけに囲まれて生活するようにしたら、毎日がとても気持ちよく送れるようになった」 (After reducing possessions as much as possible and living surrounded only by things that were truly necessary and that I liked, I was able to enjoy each day much more.)
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 2: Start by reducing your own belongings in your room.
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.explanation:
Paragraph 2 clearly states what the author first did after deciding to adopt a “possession-free lifestyle”: reducing the personal belongings in their room, such as clothes, books, and bags, while keeping only the things they needed and liked.

Question translation:
It says “decided to adopt” this lifestyle. What did the author start by doing?

Answer choices:
1. Cleaning the entire house thoroughly.
2. Reducing their personal belongings in their own room.
3. Putting away the belongings on the floor and table in the living room.
4. Moving to a room larger than the one they had used as their room before.
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author did not clean the entire house, but started with their own room.
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.why.1: (b) Correct because the first sentence of paragraph 2 clearly states: 「最初にしたのは、私の部屋にある自分の洋服や本、かばんなどを減らすことだ。」 (“The first thing I did was reduce the clothes, books, bags, and other things in my room.”)
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.why.2: (c) Incorrect because tidying the living room, including the old magazines and vacuum cleaner, occurred afterward, when the author noticed the family's belongings.
default.q.n3-13-q70-70.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the room became more spacious as a result of removing some belongings (「部屋が広くなっただけでなく」), not because the author moved to a larger room.
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 1: The author threw away belongings that their parents considered valuable and important without asking for permission.
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.explanation:
Passage 3 explains why the parents were angry: the author threw away the family's magazines and vacuum cleaner without asking their parents' permission. To the parents, the things they had paid for were valuable, and they believed in taking care of and cherishing old possessions rather than living a lifestyle of throwing things away.

Question translation:
It says that both the father and mother were angry. Why was that?

Answer choices:
1. Because "I" discarded things that the parents considered valuable and important without asking them.
2. Because "I" discarded things that the parents used frequently without asking them.
3. Because "I" discarded things that appeared to be expensive and belonged to the parents.
4. Because "I" discarded things that the parents had just bought.
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.why.0: (a) Correct because Passage 3 says that the author threw things away without asking the parents (「両親に聞かずに捨ててしまった」), while the parents considered them valuable because they had paid for them and wanted to use old belongings carefully (「みんなお金を出して買った物だから大切だ。それに、自分たちは…大切に使う生活のほうがいい」).
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the passage clearly says that no one reads the old magazines (「古い物は誰も読んでいない」) and that one vacuum cleaner is not used at all (「1台は全く使われていない」); they are not items used regularly.
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not mention whether those items appear expensive.
default.q.n3-13-q71-71.why.3: (d) Incorrect. These are old items (古い物), not things that have just been bought.
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Because the parents have different views, the author will maintain this lifestyle only within their own room.
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.explanation:
The final paragraph clearly presents the author’s thoughts and lesson: the narrator realizes that people can have different views even when they live together, and that they went too far by interfering with their parents’ belongings. From now on, the narrator will continue maintaining a “possession-free lifestyle” only within their own room.

Question translation:
What is “I” thinking now?

Answer choices:
1. A “possession-free lifestyle” is wonderful, so I must persuade my parents to start one too.
2. I realized that my parents’ way of thinking has many advantages, so I decided to give up my “possession-free lifestyle.”
3. Because my parents think differently from me, I will continue my “possession-free lifestyle” only in my own space.
4. For the time being, I will continue my “possession-free lifestyle” in my own space and wait for my parents’ views to change.
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author realized that the two sides had different views and that they had overstepped the boundary; they did not intend to make their parents do the same thing.
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author did not give up the “life without possessions”; they continue to apply it in their own life.
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.why.2: (c) Correct because the final sentence clearly states: 「一緒に住んでいても、考え方は違う。今回、私はちょっとやりすぎてしまったようだ。これからは、「持たない生活」は自分の部屋だけで実行しようと思っている。」 (Even though we live together, we think differently. This time, I seem to have gone a little too far. From now on, I intend to practice a "life without possessions" only in my own room.)
default.q.n3-13-q72-72.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author respects differences in opinion and has no intention of waiting for the parents to change their views.
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.verdict: The correct answer is 3: The author learned that receiving morning sunlight to send a signal to the body is the most important thing.
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.explanation:
**Main idea:**
The author used to think that exercising vigorously at night or bathing immediately before bed was the best way to sleep well. However, after reading a specialist's book, the author realized that getting morning sunlight is most important for sending signals to the body and regulating the sleep rhythm.

**Question translation:**
What did the author learn was most important for regulating the sleep rhythm?

**Answer choices:**
1. Bathing immediately before going to bed at night.
2. Exercising vigorously at night to make the body tired.
3. Getting morning sunlight to send signals to the body.
4. Using special equipment to exercise every day.
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.why.0: (a) Incorrect because taking a bath immediately before going to bed was only the author’s former belief (「以前の私は...寝る直前にお風呂に入ったりすればいいと思っていた」), not what the author realized was most important after reading the expert’s book.
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.why.1: (b) Incorrect because exercising intensely at night to make the body tired was also one of the author’s former misconceptions (「以前の私は、よく眠るためには夜に激しい運動をしたり...いいと思っていた」).
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states: 「しかし、専門家の本を読んでみると、睡眠のリズムを整えるには朝の光を浴びることが一番大切だと知った。朝、日光を浴びると、体に「朝が来た」という合図が送られ...」.
default.q.n3-13-q73-73.why.3: (d) Incorrect because at the end of the passage, the author clearly states that this method does not require any special tools (「特別な道具も必要なく」).
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.verdict: The correct answer is 2: The author wants to advise people who have difficulty sleeping to try taking a walk in the morning because it is easy to do.
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.explanation:
**Main idea:** The author explains that they improved their difficulty sleeping by taking a 15-minute walk in the morning to get sunlight. Since this habit is simple, easy to do, and requires no equipment, the author recommends that people experiencing sleep problems give it a try.

**Question:** What does the author most want to convey through this article?

**Choices:**
1. People troubled by sleep should immediately prepare equipment and start exercising.
2. A morning walk is easy to do, so people who do not sleep well should give it a try.
3. To regulate the sleep-wake cycle, one must sleep for at least 14 hours a day.
4. To sleep well at night, it is best to take a walk at night rather than in the morning.
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the passage clearly states that no special tools are needed (「特別な道具も必要なく」), which contradicts the idea of purchasing tools before starting.
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.why.1: (b) Correct. The passage states: 「特別な道具も必要なく、誰でも簡単にできるので、睡眠に悩んでいる人はぜひ試してみてほしい。」 This matches the author’s habit mentioned in paragraph 1: 「朝起きてすぐに15分ほど散歩をする」.
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the 14 hours in the passage refers to the period after morning sunlight exposure when the body naturally produces a substance that induces sleepiness (「その約14時間後に自然と眠くなる物質が作られる」), not to a requirement to sleep more than 14 hours a day.
default.q.n3-13-q74-74.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the author recommends taking a walk in the morning immediately after waking up to get sunlight (「朝起きてすぐに15分ほど散歩をする」), not walking at night.
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 1. おそく (遅く).
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.explanation:
Meaning: I ended up being later than last time.
- 「遅」means "late, delayed."
- Example: 夜遅くまで勉強しました。(I studied until late at night.)
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.why.0: (a) Correct. The kanji「遅」has the kun-reading「おそ(い)」; its adverbial form is「おそく」, meaning late.
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.why.1: (b) Incorrect.「きたなく」is the adverbial form of the i-adjective「汚い」(dirty).
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.why.2: (c) Incorrect.「みじかく」is the adverbial/conjunctive form of the i-adjective「短い」(short).
default.q.n3-13-q1-1.why.3: (d) Incorrect.「とおく」is the adverbial form of the i-adjective「遠い」(far, distant).
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 2. せん (線).
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.explanation:
Meaning: Use this pen to draw a straight line.
- Sino-Japanese roots:「線」(line, stroke, route).
- Example: ノートに赤い線を引きました。(I drew a red line in my notebook.)
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.why.0: (a) Incorrect.「ず」is the on-reading of「図」(as in 地図 - map, 合図 - sign).
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.why.1: (b) Correct. The kanji 「線」has the on'yomi reading 「せん」 and means a line, drawn stroke, or straight line.
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「え」is the kun-reading of 「絵」(picture, drawing).
default.q.n3-13-q2-2.why.3: (d) Incorrect.「もじ」is the reading of「文字」(written character, letter).
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ちょうさ (調査).
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.explanation:
Meaning: I plan to conduct a field survey / investigation during the summer vacation.
- Sino-Japanese readings: 「調」 +「査」 = 調査 (investigation, survey).
- Example: アンケート調査を行いました。(We conducted a questionnaire survey.)
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「査」is not read as「さつ」; do not confuse it with「察」in 観察（かんさつ）or 視察（しさつ）.
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.why.1: (b) Correct. The kanji 「調」(ちょう) combines with 「査」(さ) to form 「調査」(ちょうさ), meaning investigation or survey.
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.why.2: (c) Incorrect. 「かんさ」 is the reading of 「監査」, meaning “inspection” or “audit.”
default.q.n3-13-q3-3.why.3: (d) Incorrect.「かんさつ」is the reading of「観察」(observation).
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ゆうびん (郵便).
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.explanation:
Meaning: A parcel/letter arrived this morning.
- Kanji note:「郵」(mail) +「便」(service) = 郵便 (mail, postal service).
- Example: 郵便局で荷物を送りました。(I sent a package at the post office.)
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「郵」must contain a long vowel and be read ゆう, not ゆ, while 「便」is read びん here, not べん.
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The long vowel is missing in 「郵」; it should be read as 「ゆう」.
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.why.2: (c) Incorrect. In 「郵便」, 「便」is read as 「びん」, rather than 「べん」as in 便利 (べんり) or 雄弁 (ゆうべん).
default.q.n3-13-q4-4.why.3: (d) Correct. 郵 (on-reading ゆう) combines with 便 (びん) to give the correct reading 「ゆうびん」.
default.q.n3-13-q5-5.verdict: The correct answer is 3. こし (腰).
default.q.n3-13-q5-5.explanation:
Meaning: I had someone apply medicine to my hip/lower back.
- 「腰」: hip, waist, lower back.
- Example: 重い荷物を持って腰が痛くなりました。(My lower back began to hurt from carrying a heavy load.)
default.q.n3-13-q5-5.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「むね」 is the reading of 「胸」 (chest).
default.q.n3-13-q5-5.why.2: (c) Correct. The kanji 「腰」 has the kun-reading 「こし」 and refers to the hips, waist, or lower back.
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ほうがく (方角).
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.explanation:
Meaning: While walking along without paying much attention, I lost my sense of direction and no longer knew which way I was going.
- Sino-Japanese components: 「方」 + 「角」 = 方角 (direction, bearing).
- Example: コンパスで方角を確かめました。(I checked my direction with a compass.)
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.why.0: (a) Correct. The kanji 「方」(ほう) combines with 「角」(がく) and is correctly read 「ほうがく」, meaning direction or bearing.
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.why.1: (b) Incorrect. 「ほうこう」 is the reading of 「方向」; the second kanji is 「向」, not 「角」.
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.why.2: (c) Incorrect. The 「角」 in 「方角」 undergoes rendaku and is pronounced 「がく」, not 「かく」.
default.q.n3-13-q6-6.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 角 does not have the on-reading 「ごう」.
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.verdict: The correct answer is 3. つつんで (包んで).
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.explanation:
Meaning: Could you wrap this for me?
- Sino-Japanese reading: 「包」(BAO — to wrap, enclose).
- Example: プレゼントをきれいな紙で包みました。(I wrapped the present in beautiful paper.)
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.why.0: (a) Incorrect. 「むすんで」 is the te-form of the verb 「結ぶ」, meaning “to tie” or “to knot.”
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.why.1: (b) Incorrect.「あんで」is the te-form of the verb「編む」(to knit, to weave).
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.why.2: (c) Correct. The kanji 「包」 has the kun-reading 「つつ(む)」 (“to wrap, cover”); in the te-form, it changes to 「つつんで」.
default.q.n3-13-q7-7.why.3: (d) Incorrect. 「はこんで」 is the te-form of 「運ぶ」 (to transport, carry).
default.q.n3-13-q8-8.verdict: The correct answer is 4. ちゅうしょく (昼食).
default.q.n3-13-q8-8.explanation:
Sentence meaning: After lunch, there will be a factory tour.
- Kanji note: 昼 (daytime or noon) + 食 (eating or meal) = 昼食 (lunch).
- Example: 12時になったら昼食をとります。(I will have lunch when it becomes noon.)
