default.q.n3-26-q30-30.why.3: (d) 「小さすぎて」 means “too small” (referring to the character size), not “glare.”
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.verdict: The correct answer is 3 because 「募集」 means recruiting people to participate and naturally combines with 「参加者を募集する」.
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.explanation:
「募集（ぼしゅう）」is a noun or class 3 verb meaning “to recruit, solicit, or call for” participants, applicants, contest entries, opinions, donations, and so on. Commonly used with: 参加者／会員／社員／ボランティア／アイデアを募集する.
Example: アルバイトのスタッフを募集しています。(We are recruiting part-time staff.)
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.why.0: Wrong because gathering new students in one classroom requires 「集めた」(or「集合させた」), not 「募集」.
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.why.1: Incorrect because making coin collecting a hobby requires 「集めること」 (or 「収集すること」), not 「募集」.
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.why.2: Correct because 「募集する」(to recruit, solicit) combines naturally with 「参加者」(participants) to form 「参加者を募集する」(to recruit participants for the competition).
default.q.n3-26-q31-31.why.3: Incorrect because the city's regular collection of garbage must use 「回収しています」 (or 「集めています」/「収集しています」), not 「募集」.
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.verdict: The correct answer is 4 because 「空（から）」 refers to a container that is empty and has nothing inside, as in 「空になったビン」.
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.explanation:
「空（から）」describes a container or space whose inside is empty and contains no objects or liquid. Common uses: 空の箱 (an empty box), 空のボトル (an empty bottle), コップが空になる (for a glass to become empty).
Example: 箱を開けてみたら、中身は空だった。(When I opened the box, I found that it was completely empty.)
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.why.0: Incorrect because “a free day” should be expressed as 「空いている日」(あいているひ) or 「暇な日」, not with the noun 「空」(から).
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.why.1: Incorrect because a clichéd or shallow story is described with 「内容が薄い」, 「中身がない」, or 「空虚」; 「空」cannot be used alone in this way.
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.why.2: Incorrect. To express being away from home, use 「留守」(るす) or 「（家に）誰もいない」, not 「家が空だ」.
default.q.n3-26-q32-32.why.3: Correct because 「空（から）」 indicates that the inside of a container is empty, with nothing in it. It is precisely appropriate in 「空になったビン」 (“a bottle that has become empty”).
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.verdict: The correct answer is 1, because 「活動」refers to purposeful activities carried out by groups or individuals in society.
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.explanation:
「活動」(かつどう) means "activity" and refers to actions actively carried out by a person or organization toward a specific goal, such as social, volunteer, club, or political activities. Common expressions include: ボランティア活動, サークル活動, 政治活動, 活動を行う／する.
Example: 彼は環境を守るための活動に熱心に参加している。(He actively participates in activities to protect the environment.)
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.why.0: Correct because 「活動」 is used for social or organizational activities carried out to achieve a specific purpose; here, the purpose is to open a class introducing culture.
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.why.1: Incorrect because cleaning and doing laundry are household chores, so use 「家事」 (or 「お手伝い」), not 「活動」.
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.why.2: Incorrect because the operation of machines and elevators is expressed with 「運転」, 「稼働」, or 「作動」, not 「活動」.
default.q.n3-26-q33-33.why.3: Incorrect because frequent truck traffic or movement should be expressed with 「往来」, 「通行」, or 「行き来」. 「活動」is not used for vehicles.
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.verdict: The correct answer is 2 because 「行き先」refers to the place or destination someone is preparing to go to.
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.explanation:
「行き先（いきさき／ゆきさき）」means “destination” or “place one is headed,” referring to the specific location toward which a person or means of transportation is traveling. Common expressions include 行き先を決める (decide on a destination), 行き先を告げる (announce one’s destination), and バスの行き先 (the bus’s destination).
Example: 旅行の行き先はもう決めましたか。(Have you decided on your travel destination yet?)
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.why.0: Incorrect because the recipient’s address for a letter or email should use 「宛先」 (あてさき) or 「送信先」, not 「行き先」.
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.why.1: Correct because 「行き先」 means “the place one is going to” or “destination,” and is perfectly natural when reminding someone to report their destination before leaving the company.
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.why.2: Incorrect because asking about the direction or route to the station requires 「方向」(ほうこう) or 「この道」, not 「この行き先」.
default.q.n3-26-q34-34.why.3: Incorrect because the position ahead along a river is expressed with 「先」(さき) or 「下流」(downstream); since a river has no agency, 「行き先」is not used.
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is 2 because 「経由（けいゆ）」means passing through or stopping at an intermediate location on the way to a destination.
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.explanation:
「経由」(けいゆ) means "via, through, or by way of" and refers to passing through a place or using an intermediary person or step on the way to a destination or in order to achieve a purpose. Common expressions include: ～を経由して (via...), インターネットを経由して (through the internet), 友人を経由して (through a friend).
Example: シンガポールを経由して日本へ行きます。(I am going to Japan via Singapore.)
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.why.0: Incorrect because going through a park as a shortcut requires 「通る」(とおる) or「通り抜ける」, not「経由する」.
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.why.1: Correct because 「経由する」 is appropriately used to indicate that a means of transportation, such as a bus, passes through an intermediate stop, such as the city hall, on the way to its destination, the station.
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.why.2: Incorrect because describing going through the period or experience of working as an office employee before attending university requires 「（会社員を）経て」(へて) or 「経験して」, not 「経由」.
default.q.n3-26-q35-35.why.3: Incorrect because when a meeting continues across the lunch break, use「昼休みを挟んで」(はさんで), not「経由」.
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.verdict: The correct answer is 4. とって (わたしにとって: for me).
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.explanation:
Translation: "For me, the most important thing right now is the dog I have."
Pattern: N + にとって (for N; from N's standpoint or perspective).
Example: 家族にとって、健康が一番大切です。(For a family, health is the most important thing.)
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.why.0: (a) 対して (にたいして) means “toward/with regard to” an object affected by an action or attitude, or “in contrast to.” It is not used to introduce a subjective position or evaluation such as “as for me.”
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.why.1: (b) 比べて (にくらべて) means “compared with” and is used in a comparison between two objects, so it does not fit the meaning of the sentence.
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.why.2: (c) おいて (において) means “at, in, or within” a place, context, or field, and does not combine with わたし to express a personal viewpoint or position.
default.q.n3-27-q35-35.why.3: (d) とって (にとって) means “for” or “from the perspective of,” following a noun referring to a person or target to indicate a standpoint, viewpoint, or evaluation. It is completely correct in “for me, the most important thing is ….”
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.verdict: The correct answer is 1. でも (as in 食事でもしませんか: Would you like to get something to eat?).
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.explanation:
Translation:
A: "Would you like to go out for something to eat or drink this weekend, if you are free?"
B: "Sounds good. Let's do that!"
Pattern: N + でも (suggesting a representative example when making a casual invitation or proposal: "...or something").
Example: お茶でも飲みませんか。(Would you like to have some tea or something?)
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.why.0: (a) でも follows a noun to offer a gentle, representative example ("something like eating or drinking, for instance"). It is very commonly used in invitations and suggestions, so this is completely correct.
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.why.1: (b) では (particle で + は) emphasizes a location or means; it is not used to offer a suggested example when inviting someone.
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.why.2: (c) にも (the particles に + も) means “also in” or “also toward”; it does not form an expression meaning “go eat something.”
default.q.n3-27-q36-36.why.3: (d) にには (the particle に plus は) indicates an emphasized purpose or scope of the object (“for” or “in order to”), so it does not fit the context of making an invitation.
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.verdict: The correct answer is 2. だろう (増えるだろうと思い: thinking that it will probably increase...).
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.explanation:
Translation: “Thinking that I would have more opportunities to write once I entered elementary school, I decided to give my grandchild some stationery.”
Vocabulary—Sino-Japanese readings: 入学 (entering school), 文房具 (stationery), 孫 (grandchild).
Pattern: plain form + だろうと思う (think that something probably will...).
Example: 明日は雨が降るだろうと思い、傘を持って出かけた。(Thinking it would probably rain tomorrow, I took an umbrella with me.)
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.why.0: (a) らしい expresses an inference based on indirect information or outward impressions. It does not combine with と思い to express the speaker's subjective speculation before deciding to give a gift.
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.why.1: (b) だろう expresses the speaker's judgment or supposition about a future event (“will probably…”). The phrase ～だろうと思い (“thinking that … probably will”) is natural and correct.
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.why.2: (c) つもりだ expresses the speaker’s own intention, whereas the subject of the preceding clause is “the opportunity to write,” an objective event, so つもりだ cannot be used.
default.q.n3-27-q37-37.why.3: (d) When そうだ means “seems,” it must be combined with the masu-stem: 増えそうだ. When it follows the dictionary form, as in 増えるそうだ, it means “I hear that…,” which does not fit the speaker’s own judgment.
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.verdict: The correct answer is 2. としても (雨が降ったとしても: even if it rains / even supposing it rains).
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.explanation:
Sentence translation: "Even if it rains tomorrow, the sports festival will still be held as planned."
Pattern: plain form + としても (even if..., even though...; expressing a concessive hypothetical condition).
Example: たとえ失敗したとしても、後悔はしない。(Even if I fail, I will not regret it.)
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.why.0: (a) としたら means "if it were the case that..." and is used for a favorable hypothetical condition followed by an expected result or judgment. It is not used in a sentence expressing contrast or concession, such as "even if it rains, the event will be held."
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.why.1: (b) Correct. としても means “even if,” “even though,” or “although.” It expresses a contrary condition: the action in the following clause still takes place despite the assumption in the preceding clause.
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.why.2: (c) とすると means “assuming that...,” expressing a favorable or straightforward conditional assumption; the following clause cannot express a contrasting action.
default.q.n3-27-q38-38.why.3: (d) とするなら means “if we assume that...” and is also used for favorable conditions, so it does not fit the contrastive meaning of the sentence.
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.verdict: The correct answer is 1. こんなに (こんなにおいしいのに: even though it is this delicious...).
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.explanation:
Translation:
Tanaka: "I cannot eat cheese. Ms. Yamashita, please have it if you would like."
Yamashita: "Thanks. Wow, this is delicious. If it tastes this good, why can't you eat it?"
Pattern: こんなに + adjective / verb (to this extent, at this level); indicates a degree directly experienced or perceived by the speaker.
Example: こんなにたくさん食べられません。(I cannot eat this much.)
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.why.0: (a) こんなに means “to this extent” or “this much,” referring to a quality directly connected to the speaker’s immediate experience (Yamashita has just eaten a piece of cheese and directly experienced how delicious it is), so it is completely appropriate.
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.why.1: (b) そんなに means “to that extent” or “that much,” referring to something associated with the listener or something reported by someone else; it is inappropriate when the speaker is directly experiencing and praising something.
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.why.2: (c) あんなに means “to such an extent” or “that much,” referring to something distant from both the speaker and listener, whether in the past or at a distance, so it does not fit the present context.
default.q.n3-27-q39-39.why.3: (d) どんなに means “how ...” or “no matter how ...” and is commonly used in exclamatory or concessive patterns such as どんなに～ても. It does not directly combine with ～のに in this context.
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.verdict: The correct answer is 3. に／に (おすしにカレーにラーメン: sushi, curry, ramen, and so on).
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.explanation:
Sentence translation:
A: "The sushi restaurant we're going to has everything—sushi, curry, ramen, and more."
B: "It sounds like an interesting restaurant."
Structure: N1 に N2 (に...) (things such as ... and ...; used to list multiple nouns and emphasize variety and abundance).
Example: 机の上には、本にノートに辞書が山積みになっている。(The desk is piled high with books, notebooks, dictionaries, and more.)
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.why.0: (a) で／で: The particle で is not repeated between nouns to list items in the sense of "things such as... and...".
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.why.1: (b) が／が: the particle が marks the subject or an object of perception, and it is not repeated between nouns to add items in a list.
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.why.2: (c) に／に: The pattern N1 に N2 (に N3 ...) lists a variety of objects or events (“things such as N1 and N2 ...”), fitting the following clause meaning “there is every kind of dish.”
default.q.n3-27-q40-40.why.3: (d) は／は: The particle は marks the topic or emphasizes contrast; it is not used to list multiple nouns.
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 近ければ (近ければ近いほど: the closer..., the more...).
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.explanation:
Translation:
Staff: “What kind of room are you looking for?”
Customer: “I’d like an inexpensive room near the station.”
Staff: “Hmm, that may be difficult. The closer it is to the station, the more expensive the room will be.”
Pattern: A-ければ A-いほど / V-れば V-るほど (the more..., the more...).
Example: 日本語は勉強すればするほど面白くなります。(The more you study Japanese, the more interesting it becomes.)
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.why.0: (a) 近いから indicates a reason (“because it is near”) and cannot be combined with [adjective + ほど] to form a proportional comparison pattern.
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.why.1: (b) 近くて is the connective te-form (“near and...”) and does not form the “the more..., the more...” construction.
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.why.2: 近くても expresses concession (“even though it is near”) and does not combine with ほど in a correlative comparative structure.
default.q.n3-27-q41-41.why.3: (d) 近ければ is the ば-conditional form of the -i adjective 近い (近い → 近ければ). It correctly forms the pattern [A-ければ A-いほど], meaning “the more..., the more...”.
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.verdict: The correct answer is 2. 思い出せなくて (どうしてもタイトルが思い出せなくて: no matter how hard I tried, I could not remember the title).
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.explanation:
Translation:
A: "The movie I watched the other day was really good, but I just can't remember its title no matter how hard I try."
B: "What kind of movie was it?"
Structure: どうしても + negative potential-form verb (no matter what, cannot...).
Example: 彼の名前をどうしても思い出せない。(I just cannot remember his name no matter how hard I try.)
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.why.0: (a) 思い出せそうで means “seemingly about to remember,” and does not naturally combine with どうしても, which is usually used with a negative expression to mean “no matter how hard one tries, one cannot…”.
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.why.1: (b) 思い出せなくて is the negative potential て-form: 思い出せる → 思い出せない → 思い出せなくて. Combined with どうしても, it means “no matter what, I cannot remember,” and is used at the end of a sentence as a mild explanation or apology. It is completely accurate.
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.why.2: (c) 思い出してきて means “gradually remembering” or “starting to remember,” which is the opposite of the context of forgetting the movie’s title.
default.q.n3-27-q42-42.why.3: (d) 思い出させないで is a mildly prohibitive causative form meaning “please don’t make me remember,” so it is completely wrong for the meaning and conversational context.
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.verdict: The correct answer is 1. 借りられます (どなたでも借りられますよ: anyone can borrow it).
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.explanation:
A: “Yes, Minami Library speaking.”
B: “Excuse me, can anyone borrow books from your library?”
A: “Anyone who lives in Minami City can borrow them.”
Pattern: V-られる (potential form: can do something).
Example: 会員になれば、どなたでも施設を利用できます。(If you become a member, anyone can use the facilities.)
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.why.0: (a) 借りられます is the potential form of the verb 借りる (to borrow), used to answer the question of whether residents/customers can borrow books; it is completely correct.
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.why.1: (b) 借りてくださいます means “will you borrow it for me?”—the honorific form of てくれる. This is semantically incorrect because borrowing it is the customer’s entitlement, not a favor being requested from someone else.
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.why.2: (c) お借りいたします is a special humble expression (お＋V-ます＋いたす), used only for the speaker's own action, here the library employee's action; it is not used for the action of a customer or member of the public (どなたでも).
default.q.n3-27-q43-43.why.3: (d) お借りいただきます (お＋V-ます＋いただく) is used when asking or requesting the listener to borrow something; it is not used to state the benefit or possibility of being allowed to borrow a book.
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.verdict: The correct answer is 4. にまで (お隣にまで聞こえるよ: it’s loud enough for the neighbors to hear it).
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.explanation:
Dialogue translation:
Father: "Hiroshi, stop playing music so loudly. The sound is carrying all the way to the neighbors’ house."
Hiroshi: "Oh, I’m sorry, Dad."
Structure: N + にまで (all the way to / even as far as N, emphasizing an unexpectedly or undesirably wide range).
Example: 彼の噂は隣のクラスにまで広がっている。(The rumors about him have spread even to the neighboring class.)
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.why.0: (a) までで is the combination of まで and で, indicating the range or means up to which something stops. It does not combine with 聞こえる, a verb describing perception or the transmission of sound.
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.why.1: (b) でまで emphasizes the place where an action takes place (“even at ...”), but the verb 聞こえる takes the particle に to indicate the object or place where the sound is heard.
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.why.2: (c) までに indicates the final deadline by which an action must be completed (“by” or “no later than”), so it does not fit the context.
default.q.n3-27-q44-44.why.3: (d) にまで combines the particle に, indicating the object or direction toward which the sound is heard with 聞こえる, and まで, emphasizing that it spreads as far as an undesirable place: “even as far as…” It is completely accurate.
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.verdict: The correct answer is 2. ついたり消えたり (ついたり消えたりしている: repeatedly turning on and off, flickering).
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.explanation:
Sentence translation: “The living-room light keeps flickering on and off, so please go buy a new light bulb.”
Vocabulary and kanji: 居間 (いま: living room/common room), 電球 (でんきゅう: light bulb).
Structure: V1-たり V2-たりする (sometimes..., sometimes...; describes alternating contrasting actions or states).
Example: 星がピカピカついたり消えたりしている。(The stars keep glittering on and off.)
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.why.0: (a) ついたり消えて is grammatically incorrect because repeated alternating actions require both clauses to use the たり-form (it should be ついたり消えたりする).
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.why.1: (b) 一応 (いちおう: anyway; for the time being) correctly uses the matching intransitive verbs つく (to turn on) and 消える (to go off) with the particle が (電気が), combined in the [V1-たり V2-たりする] pattern to express a repeatedly flickering state. It is completely correct.
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.why.2: (c) つけたり消して is incorrect both in particle usage (the transitive verbs つける and 消す cannot take 電気が as their subject) and in grammar (たり is missing from the second clause).
default.q.n3-27-q45-45.why.3: (d) つけたり消したり consists of the transitive verbs つける (“turn on”) and 消す (“turn off”), describing deliberate actions performed by a person and requiring the particle を. It does not fit the natural-subject phrase 電気が.
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 動かなくなるまえに (体が動かなくなるまえに: before your body can no longer move or walk).
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.explanation:
Translation: Saying, “Dad wants to travel before he gets too old and weak to get around,” my father went abroad last month.
Vocabulary & Sino-Japanese readings: 年を取る (としをとる: to grow old), 海外 (かいがい: overseas, abroad).
Pattern: V-る + まえに (before doing something / before a state occurs).
Example: 暗くなるまえに、家に帰りましょう。(Let’s go home before it gets dark.)
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.why.0: (a) 動かさないあいだに uses the transitive verb 動かさない (“not move something”), which does not fit the particle が with 体が. Also, あいだに does not correctly express the meaning “before a change occurs.”
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.why.1: 動かさないうちに incorrectly uses the transitive verb; when うちに means “while one still can,” the affirmative form must be used: 動くうちに or 元気なうちに.
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.why.2: (c) 動かなくなるまえに correctly combines the intransitive verb describing a change of state (動く → 動かなくなる: to become unable to move or function) with まえに (“before”), expressing the desire to travel before one’s health deteriorates.
default.q.n3-27-q46-46.why.3: (d) 動かなくなるころに means “around the time when the body can no longer move,” which is completely contrary to the purpose of traveling while still healthy.
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 行われるところです (これから開会式が行われるところです: The opening ceremony is about to be held).
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.explanation:
Translation:
A: “Has the match started yet?”
B: “The opening ceremony is about to begin now.”
Vocabulary and kanji meanings: 開会式 (opening ceremony), 試合 (match).
Pattern: これから + V-る + ところです (be about to do something right now).
Example: これから昼ご飯を食べるところです。(I am about to eat lunch now.)
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.why.0: (a) 行っているところです uses an active transitive verb, which does not agree with 開会式が, and the ～ているところ pattern indicates an action in progress, contrary to the near-future adverb これから (about to).
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.why.1: (b) 行われているところです correctly uses the passive voice, but it is combined with ～ているところ (in the middle of happening), which conflicts with これから, an adverb indicating that something is about to begin.
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.why.2: (c) 行われるところです combines the passive form 行われる (“be held,” appropriate for the subject 開会式が) with the pattern [V-る + ところです] (“be about to do”), fitting perfectly with the adverb これから. It is completely correct.
default.q.n3-27-q47-47.why.3: (d) 行うところです uses the active form of the transitive verb 行う, so it cannot be used with the particle が and the event noun 開会式が; 行われる is required.
default.q.n3-27-q48-48.verdict: The correct order is: 3 → 2 → 4 → 1. The ★ position is answer choice 4 (家にいる).

Complete dialogue:
配達員「お荷物の配達時間ですが、明日の夜8時ごろでいかがですか。」
客「その時間は多分家にいると思うので大丈夫です。お願いします。」

Delivery person: “Regarding the delivery time for your package, would around 8 p.m. tomorrow be convenient?”

default.q.n3-27-q48-48.why.0: (a) 1. と思う: It is in the fourth position (the final blank), immediately before the conjunction expressing cause or reason 「ので」, forming「～と思うので」(because I think that...).
default.q.n3-27-q48-48.why.1: (b) 2. 多分: In the second position, this conjectural adverb means “probably” or “perhaps.” It comes before the predicate 「家にいる」 and combines with 「と思う」 at the end of the sentence.
default.q.n3-27-q48-48.why.2: (c) 3. 時間は: Belongs in position 1, following the 「その」already at the beginning of the sentence to form the time phrase 「その時間は」(during that time).

default.q.n3-27-q49-49.explanation:
Complete sentence:
山下「田中さん、ABC大学のリュウ先生を知っていますか。」
田中「お名前は開いたことがありますが、会ったことはありません。」

Yamashita: "Tanaka, do you know Professor Ryu at ABC University?"
Tanaka: "I have heard the name, but I have never met him in person."

default.q.n3-27-q49-49.why.1: (b) 2. 会ったことは: It is in the fourth position and comes directly before the negative predicate 「ありません」 already provided at the end of the sentence, forming the experience pattern 「～たことはありません」 (“have never met”).
default.q.n3-27-q49-49.why.2: (c) 3. 開いたことが: It appears in position 2 (after hearing or learning someone's name), follows the topic 「お名前は」, and combines with 「ありますが」to form 「～たことがある」(have ever...).
default.q.n3-27-q49-49.why.3: (d) 4. お名前は: It is in the first position, placing the noun at the beginning as an emphasized topic with the particle「は」, in contrast with the following clause「会ったことは」.

Complete sentence:
わたしがもっとも行ってみたい寺のひとつの京都の高山寺がある。

Meaning:
"One of the temples I most want to visit is Kozan-ji Temple in Kyoto."
default.q.n3-27-q50-50.why.0: (a) 1. 行ってみたい: It is in the second position, where the「～てみたい」verb form follows the adverb「もっとも」and modifies the noun「寺」in the next position.
default.q.n3-27-q50-50.why.1: (b) 2. ひとつに: Occupying the fourth position, it follows 「寺の」 and comes before the predicate 「京都の高山寺がある」, forming the structure 「～の ひとつに ... がある」 (one of the ... is ...).
default.q.n3-27-q50-50.why.2: (c) 3. もっとも: It is in position 1 and is an adverb expressing the highest degree (“the most”), directly modifying 「行ってみたい」 after the subject 「わたしが」.
default.q.n3-27-q50-50.why.3: (d) 4. 寺の: It is in the third position (★), where the noun 「寺」 is modified by the relative clause 「わたしがもっとも行ってみたい」 and connected to 「ひとつ」 by the possessive particle 「の」.

Complete sentence:
「プレゼント」という映画を見て、この映画ほど人生について考えさせられる映画はないと思った。

After watching the film 「プレゼント」, I thought that no other film had ever made me reflect on life as much as this one.

default.q.n3-27-q51-51.why.1: (b) 2. について: It occupies the third position (the ★ slot), follows the noun 「人生」 to form the pattern 「～について」 (about something), and modifies the verb 「考えさせられる」.
default.q.n3-27-q51-51.why.2: (c) 3. 人生: It occupies the second position and is the noun that combines with the following 「について」 to form the phrase 「人生について」 (about life).
default.q.n3-27-q51-51.why.3: (d) 4. 考えさせられる: It occupies the fourth position and is a causative-passive verb that directly modifies the noun 「映画」 already present in the following clause 「映画はない」.
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.verdict: The correct order is: 2 → 4 → 3 → 1. ★ is answer choice 3 (ということを).
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.explanation:
Complete sentence:
友だちからのメールが来るまで今日がレポートのしめ切り日だったということをすっかり忘れていた。

Meaning:
"I had completely forgotten that today was the report deadline until I received an email from my friend."
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.why.0: (a) 1. すっかり忘れていた: It is in the fourth position at the end of the sentence and serves as the main predicate, following the object particle「を」to form「～ということをすっかり忘れていた」.
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.why.1: (b) 2. メールが来るまで: Placed in the first position, it follows「友だちからの」to form the time adverbial「友だちからのメールが来るまで」(until an email from a friend arrives).
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.why.2: (c) 3. ということを: In position 3 (the ★ slot), it nominalizes the clause 「今日がレポートのしめ切り日だった」 and makes it the object of 「忘れていた」.
default.q.n3-27-q52-52.why.3: (d) 4. 今日がレポートのしめ切り日だった: It is in the second position and is the statement clause placed before 「ということを」.
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.verdict: The correct answer is 4. それとも.
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.explanation: Before the blank, the author asks: 「先輩や友達が間違っているのでしょうか」(Could my seniors and friends be using it incorrectly?). Immediately after the blank comes a second question: 「わたしが習ったことがまちがっているのでしょか」(Or could what I learned be wrong?). These are two contrasting possibilities presented as a choice (A or B). The most suitable conjunction to connect the two questions is 「それとも」 (or, or perhaps).
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.why.0: (a) 「ところで」(by the way, incidentally) is used to shift to a new topic that is not directly related. It is not used to present alternatives in a question asking whether it is A or B.
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.why.1: (b) 「ところが」 (however, but) connects to an unexpected actual result that contrasts with the usual expectation; it is not used to connect two interrogative sentences.
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.why.2: (c) 「それなら」 (“in that case”) introduces a conclusion or suggestion based on the premise just mentioned. It is not suitable for presenting an opposing choice.
default.q.n3-27-q53-53.why.3: (d) 「それとも」(or, or else) is a conjunction used to connect two alternative questions (「～でしょうか。それとも、～でしょうか」). It fits the context of being unsure whether the senior made a mistake or whether the speaker studied incorrectly.
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 言われました.
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.explanation: Based on the following sentence: 「起きてすぐに来たから、間違えて『おはよう。』と言ったのだと思いました」 (I thought that because he had just woken up and come straight here, he had accidentally said “Ohayou”), the person who performed the greeting 「おはよう」 was the senior. Therefore, from the author’s perspective (as the person who heard the greeting), the appropriate pattern is the passive form: 「先輩に『おはよう。』と言われました」 (My senior said “Ohayou” to me / I was told “Ohayou” by my senior).
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.why.0: (a) 「言いました」 (active: said) is incorrect because the following sentence clearly states that the author thought the senior had accidentally misspoken, showing that the senior—not the author—was the person who greeted the author.
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.why.1: (b) 「言わせました」 means “made or allowed someone to speak” as a causative, which does not fit the meaning or the interaction between a junior and a senior.
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.why.2: (c) 「言われました」(was told / was spoken to) fits the passive pattern 「[person] に～と言われる」, expressing that the author was greeted with 「おはよう」by a senior colleague in the afternoon.
default.q.n3-27-q54-54.why.3: (d) 「言えました」 (potential form: “was able to say”) does not fit the meaning of the context or the particle structure 「先輩に」.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.verdict: The correct answer is 1. ついたのです.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.explanation: The expression 「気がつく」 means "to realize / notice." In the passage, the author describes how events unfolded: at first, the author thought only one senior student had misspoken, but later noticed that many other people around them spoke the same way. The sentence ending 「～のです」 (past form 「～たのです」) provides an explanatory, narrative tone for naturally describing events in writing. The choices containing 「から/せい/おかげ」 all express cause and effect, so they do not fit this context.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.why.0: (a) 「ついたのです」 correctly combines the fixed expression 「気がつく」 (to realize, notice) with the sentence ending 「～のです」, which provides an explanation of the development of the realization in the passage.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.why.1: (b) 「ついたからです」 (“because I realized it”) is incorrect because it does not explain the reason for a preceding result.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.why.2: (c) 「ついたせいです」 (“because of ...,” resulting in a bad outcome) is incorrect both grammatically and semantically because the sentence does not state a cause of a negative consequence.
default.q.n3-27-q55-55.why.3: (d) 「ついたおかげです」 (thanks to... bringing about a good result) is semantically incorrect because the preceding clause is not a cause that produces a favorable result in the following clause.
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.verdict: The correct answer is 2. その.
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.explanation: Earlier, in the second paragraph, the author mentioned that a senior student at school greeted them with 「おはよう」 in the afternoon (「学校で先輩に『おはよう。』と言われました」). After friends explained that people working at 24-hour workplaces such as convenience stores often use this greeting when starting a shift, the author made the connection: 「確かに、その先輩もコンビニで働いていています」 (Indeed, that senior student also works at a convenience store). The demonstrative 「その」refers to the person mentioned earlier in the context.
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.why.0: (a) 「以下の」(below; following) introduces information that will be listed afterward. It cannot be used as an attributive modifier for a person mentioned earlier.
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.why.1: (b) 「その」 (“that”) is a demonstrative referring to something mentioned in the preceding paragraph (the senior who said “Ohayou” in the afternoon in paragraph 2).
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.why.2: (c) 「留学した」 (“studied abroad”) is incorrect because the person who studied abroad was the author, a Korean international student, whereas the senpai was Japanese (「日本人の先輩」).
default.q.n3-27-q56-56.why.3: (d) 「驚いた」(was surprised) is incorrect because the author, not the senior person, was surprised by this way of greeting.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.verdict: The correct answer is 4. 知りました.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.explanation: The concluding section summarizes what the author realized after the experience: 「先輩や友達がなぜ朝ではないのに『おはよう』を使っているのか、わかりました。そして、教室で習ったのとは違う使い方もあるということを知りました。」 (I understood why seniors and friends use “ohayō” even when it is not morning. I also learned that it has uses different from what we learned in class.) The corresponding structures, 「～わかりました。そして、～知りました」, clearly and accurately express the writer’s acquisition of new understanding.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.why.0: (a) 「知ったのでしょう」 expresses a supposition about someone else's action or a probing question (“I suppose they found out”), so it is not used to state the writer's own realization in the first person.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.why.1: (b) 「知るはずです」 expresses a well-founded prediction or inference (“should know”), so it does not fit recounting an actual experience that has already occurred.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.why.2: (c) 「知っていました」 (“already knew”) conflicts with the flow of the passage because the author initially did not know this usage and was very surprised, realizing it only after asking friends.
default.q.n3-27-q57-57.why.3: (d) 「知りました」 (came to know) describes the author's own acquisition of new knowledge or awareness after the event, pairing perfectly with 「わかりました」 in the preceding clause.
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.verdict: The correct answer is 3. 一生の仕事だな (This is the work I will do for the rest of my life).
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.explanation:
- Main point of the passage:
The passage explains the craft-related saying 「三日、三月、三年」 (3 days, 3 months, 3 years): if you can persevere for 3 days, you can continue for 3 months; if you can persevere for 3 months, you can continue for 3 years; and once you have passed the 3-year mark, you can keep doing it forever (ずっと続けられる). After Mr. Hayashi had passed the 3-year mark (三年を過ぎた頃), he also began to feel that this was the work he would devote his life to (一生の仕事だな).

- Question translation:
Which phrase belongs in 「(　　 )」?

- Answer choices:
1. お客が増えたな: The number of customers has increased.
2. 0年は続けよう (originally 20年は続けよう): Let’s keep doing this for 20 years.
3. 一生の仕事だな: This is the work I’ll do for the rest of my life.
4. 三年間がんばろう: Let’s work hard for three years.
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.why.0: (a) Choice 1, 「お客が増えたな」, is incorrect because the passage does not mention an increase in the number of customers or the restaurant’s business situation at all.
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.why.1: (b) Choice 2, 「0年は続けよう」 (the original question is 「20年は続けよう」), is incorrect. Although the opening mentions 「20年以上寿司をにぎっている林さん」, this refers to the number of years he has actually worked up to the present, not a goal set when he had just passed the three-year mark. The proverb emphasizes continuing forever after three years, rather than setting a specific time limit.
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.why.2: (c) Choice 3 「一生の仕事だな」 is the correct answer. Direct evidence from the passage: 「そして三年我慢できればずっと続けられという意味だ。林さんも三年を過ぎた頃「（　　）」と思えるようになった。」 Here, “ずっと続けられる” (being able to continue forever) is synonymous with “一生の仕事” (a lifelong job).
default.q.n3-27-q58-58.why.3: (d) Choice 4 「三年間がんばろう」 is incorrect because the time referred to is 「三年を過ぎた頃」 (“around the time three years had passed”). Therefore, it cannot be a thought about starting to work hard for the next three years.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.verdict: The correct answer is 3: Items that cannot be repaired immediately can be kept for later repair, and the repair is completely free of charge.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.explanation:
Summary of the passage:
In addition to lending books, Yamada Library holds a “Toy Hospital” on the third Saturday of every month. Specialists repair broken or nonworking toys free of charge. If a repair requires more time, they may keep the toy and work on it at their convenience. To ease children’s anxiety about leaving behind a favorite toy, they tell them that the toy is seriously ill and needs to be “hospitalized,” which reassures the children when they hand it over.

Translation of the question:
Which of the following statements about this “Toy Hospital” is correct?

Translation of the choices:
1. Because toys can also be “hospitalized,” children feel reassured when they themselves have to be hospitalized.
2. For broken or nonworking toys, they repair only those that can be fixed immediately on-site.
3. Toys that cannot be repaired immediately may also be kept for repair, and this does not cost anything.
4. Because Yamada Library becomes a toy hospital on the third Saturday, books cannot be borrowed at all that day.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.why.0: (a) Incorrect. In the article, saying that a toy “has to be hospitalized” (入院) is merely a metaphor to reassure children when they leave their toys with a repair specialist. It does not mean that the children are hospitalized and bring the toys with them.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.why.1: (b) Incorrect. The passage clearly states: 「直すのに時間がかかる場合は、預かってゆっくり修理することもあります」 (When repairs take a long time, they may keep the item and repair it carefully), so they do not repair only items that can be fixed immediately on-site.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.why.2: (c) Correct. The passage states "プロが無料で修理します" (A professional will repair it free of charge) and "直すのに時間がかかる場合は、預かってゆっくり修理することもあります" (If the repair takes time, the item may be kept and repaired carefully). Because the service is free, the customer does not have to pay even if the item is kept for repair.
default.q.n3-27-q59-59.why.3: (d) Incorrect. The passage begins: "本の貸し出しのほかに毎月第3土曜日に「おもちや病院」を開いています" (In addition to lending books, we open a “Toy Hospital” on the third Saturday of every month). This means that book lending continues as usual; it is not forbidden all day.

default.q.n3-27-q61-61.verdict: The correct answer is 4: ろうそくの光によって、心や体を休ませようとする人が多くなっているから.
default.q.n3-27-q61-61.explanation:
**Main point:** The passage explains that candles are becoming increasingly popular because their orange light helps calm the mind and relieve mental stress and physical fatigue. In an increasingly anxious society, more and more people are turning to candlelight to relax both mentally and physically.

**Translation of the question:**
The passage mentions that candles are becoming popular. What is said to be the reason?

**Translation of the answer choices:**
1. Because the number of people who like candlelight has increased, candles sell all year round.
2. Because people have begun to realize that candlelight makes them energetic and active.
3. Because more and more people want to use candlelight to make an anxious society brighter.
4. Because more and more people want to relax and rest their minds and bodies with candlelight.
default.q.n3-27-q61-61.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the fact that candles are sold year-round and that more people enjoy candlelight is a phenomenon stated in the introduction, not an explanation of why candles are popular.
default.q.n3-27-q61-61.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is incorrect because making people more active (人を活動的にさせる) is an effect of the white light from fluorescent lamps (蛍光灯の白い光), not of candles.
default.q.n3-27-q61-61.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 is incorrect because the passage says that people living in an uneasy society turn to candles for comfort. It does not say that candlelight is used to make society brighter.
default.q.n3-27-q61-61.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct based on the sentence: 「ろうそくなどのオレンジ色の光は、心を落ち着かせ、ストレスや体の疲れを取ってくれるらしい。不安の多い社会の中で、こういう効果に期待してろうそくに火をつける人が増えているようである。」 This shows that people light candles because they hope for an effect that relaxes the mind and body (心や体を休ませる).
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (寝させてほしい).
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.explanation:
- Main point of the passage: Early in the morning at a hotel in the countryside, the father is woken up by his three-year-old daughter. However, because he is still too sleepy to open his eyes, he pulls the blanket back over himself and says, "Just a little longer," implying that he wants to keep sleeping for a little while.
- Question translation: Which phrase best expresses the speaker's feelings following ①「もうすこし」(a little longer)?
- Translation of the choices:
  1. Want to be woken up early
  2. Want to get up early / want someone to get up early
  3. Want to be allowed to keep sleeping (Let me sleep a little longer)
  4. Want someone not to sleep
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.why.0: (a) Choice 1 does not fit because “I” (the father) is still sleepy and wants to sleep longer, not because he wants his daughter to wake him up early (早く起こしてほしい).
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 does not fit because “早く起きてほしい” (I want you to get up early) is the daughter's remark when waking her father (「おとうさん、早く起きて」), not the father's feelings.
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is correct because the passage says: 「まだまだ目が覚めないわたしは①『もうすこし』といってふとんをかぶる」 (I was still not fully awake, so I said “a little longer” and pulled the futon over me), expressing the desire to sleep a little longer (もうすこし寝させてほしい).
default.q.n3-27-q62-62.why.3: (d) Choice 4 does not fit because「寝ないでほしい」(I want you not to sleep) is completely opposite to the father's action of covering himself with a blanket because he wanted to keep sleeping.
default.q.n3-27-q63-63.explanation:
- Main point: The three-year-old girl watches the vivid red dawn early in the morning but does not yet know the word 「朝焼け」. She uses the word for a red sky that she does know, 「夕焼け」, to creatively form 「夕焼けの朝」 (a sunset-like morning) and call her father over to look.
- Question translation: Which word corresponds to ②, “the Japanese word that she herself knows”?
- Answer choices:
  1. 「朝焼け」 (red dawn / dawn glow)
  2. 「夕焼け」 (red sunset / evening glow)
  3. 「きれい」 (beautiful)
  4. 「おとうさん」 (father)
default.q.n3-27-q63-63.why.0: (a) Choice 1 does not fit because the text clearly states that the girl did not know this word: 「娘は3歳。『朝焼け』ということばは知らなかったが」(My daughter was three years old. Although she did not know the word "朝焼け"...).
default.q.n3-27-q63-63.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is correct because, upon seeing the bright red early-morning sky, the child did not know the word 「朝焼け」 but used the familiar word 「夕焼け」 to say: 「夕焼けの朝だよ」. The passage states: 「『朝焼け』ということばは知らなかったが、②自分の知っている日本語で目の前に広がる美しい景色を上手に伝えることができた」.
default.q.n3-27-q63-63.why.2: (c) Answer choice 3 does not fit because "きれい" is simply an adjective meaning beautiful; it is not the vocabulary the girl uses to name the phenomenon of the vividly red sky instead of "朝焼け".
default.q.n3-27-q63-63.why.3: (d) Choice 4 does not fit because 「おとうさん」 is a term used to address one's father and has no connection with describing natural scenery.
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (「わたし」は、娘が自分の知っていることばできれいな景色を伝えたことに感動した。).
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.explanation:
- Main point: After hearing his daughter use the amusing expression 「夕焼けの朝」 to describe a beautiful sunrise, the father wakes up and looks out the window. He is deeply moved by his daughter’s ability to express emotions through language, as well as by the human capacity for linguistic expression in general.
- Question translation: Which of the following is consistent with the passage?
- Answer choices:
  1. Although “I” was awakened by my daughter, I could not fully wake up and did not get up until the evening.
  2. “I” was moved because my daughter used the words she knew to convey a beautiful scene.
  3. “I” was happy because my daughter told me that there was a beautiful sunset outside the window.
  4. “I” strongly thought that one day my daughter would also be able to express her feelings.
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.why.0: (a) Answer choice 1 does not fit because immediately after hearing his daughter say "夕焼けの朝だよ", the father got up in the morning, rather than sleeping until evening and only then waking up (夕方になってやっと起きた).
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is correct because the passage expresses the father's emotion and conclusion: 「自分の知っている日本語で目の前に広がる美しい景色を上手に伝えることができた。人はだれでもことばを使って自分の気持ちを表す力を持っている、わたしはそう感じた」.
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.why.2: (c) Choice 3 does not fit because the actual view outside the window was the morning dawn sky (「美しい朝焼けの空だ」), not a sunset (夕焼け).
default.q.n3-27-q64-64.why.3: (d) Choice 4 does not fit because the father noticed that the girl was already very good at expressing her emotions at age three. He did not speculate or expect that “one day she would eventually be able to do it” (いつか...できるようになるだろう).
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.verdict: The correct answer is choice 4: It is important to explore and improve the way the email is presented so that it is easier to read.
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.explanation:
- Summary: The passage points out that writing an easy-to-understand email may seem simple but is actually difficult. It then raises a question and offers specific advice on how to organize an email so that it is easy to read and understand.
- Question translation: What does the author say about email in this passage?
- Answer choices:
  1. Email is convenient because it can be sent at a convenient time.
  2. Email recipients can choose what they want to read.
  3. Email is harder to read than handwritten letters or FAXes.
  4. Writers should explore and improve their writing methods to make emails easier to read.
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.why.0: (a) Answer choice 1 is incorrect because the article says that the recipient can read the message at a convenient time (「相手の都合がいいときに相手に読んでもらうことができます」), not that the sender can send the email at a convenient time.
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.why.1: (b) Answer choice 2 is incorrect because the passage says that readers can choose when to read (「時間を選んで読めます」), not which content or letter they want to read.
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage does not compare email as being harder to read than handwritten letters or FAX.
default.q.n3-27-q65-65.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is correct because the author raises the question: 「読みやすいメールを書くには、どのような工夫が必要でしょうか」 (What techniques are needed to write easy-to-read emails?), and then presents a series of email-writing rules for readers to apply.
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: The point not mentioned (and therefore incorrect according to the passage) is “writing especially important matters at the very beginning of the email.”
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.explanation:
- Summary: The passage lists email-writing rules: avoid making a line too long by breaking lines appropriately, leave a blank line when changing topics, repeat important information at the end, and include your full name and contact details (email address, phone number, and FAX number) at the end of the message.
- Question translation: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage?
- Answer choices:
  1. Avoid making a line too long.
  2. Write particularly important information at the very beginning of the email.
  3. Leave a blank line when changing topics in the middle.
  4. Include your name, email address, phone number, and FAX number at the end.
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is mentioned in the passage: 「まず、一行の文字数を多くしないで、短く切って次の行に進むようにしましょう」(First, do not put too many characters on one line; break it into shorter lines and continue on the next line).
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.why.1: (b) Choice 2 is not mentioned in the passage and contradicts its content. The author advises: 「特に重要なことは、文章の最後にももう一度書いたほうがいい」 (Things that are particularly important should be written once again at the end), not at the very beginning (一番最初).
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is mentioned in the passage: 「一つの内容を書き終わったら。次の一行は何も書かないで、その次の行から書き始めます」 (When you finish writing one piece of content, leave the next line blank and start writing from the line after that).
default.q.n3-27-q66-66.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is mentioned in the passage: 「文章を全部書き終わったら、自分の名前と連絡先を書きます... メールアドレスのほかに自分の電話番号とFAX番号も知らせておきましょう」 (“After finishing writing the entire document, write your name and contact information... In addition to your email address, also provide your telephone and FAX numbers”).
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.verdict: The correct answer is choice 2: It should be corrected by making one line shorter (breaking the lines appropriately).
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.explanation:
- Summary: Based on the email-formatting principles explained in the passage (short line breaks, blank lines when changing topics, repeating important information at the end, and including complete contact information), the correct revision is to make each line of text shorter.
- Question translation: According to the passage, how should the email below be revised?
- Answer choices:
  1. Do not write about the same content twice.
  2. Make each line shorter.
  3. Do not include a telephone or fax number.
  4. Increase the spacing between lines even more.
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.why.0: (a) Choice 1 is incorrect because the passage recommends repeating important points at the end of the writing (「特に重要なことは、文章の最後にももう一度書いたほうがいい」), rather than prohibiting repetition.
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.why.1: (b) Option 2 is correct because the passage states: 「一行の文字数を多くしないで、短く切って次の行に進むようにしましょう」(Do not put too many characters on one line; keep it short and continue on the next line).
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.why.2: (c) Choice 3 is incorrect because the passage advises including both a phone number and a FAX number (「メールアドレスのほかに自分の電話番号とFAX番号も知らせておきましょう」).
default.q.n3-27-q67-67.why.3: (d) Choice 4 is incorrect because the passage only instructs the writer to leave one blank line when changing topics (「次の一行は何も書かないで」); it does not require increased line spacing.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.verdict: The correct answer is 4: Because they wanted to know what the white thing was.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.explanation:
Main point: While taking a walk in the park, the author saw many white things in a tree in the distance that looked like snow. Curious about what they were (何かと思って), the author went closer to take a look.

Question translation: In the phrase “went closer to take a look,” why did the author go closer?
Answer choices:
1. To admire the beautiful leaves from a closer distance.
2. To find out the name of the tree with white flowers.
3. To look at the snow from a closer distance.
4. To find out what the white things were.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.why.0: (a) Incorrect because the author approached the object to find out what the snow-white substance stuck to the tree was, not to admire the leaves from a closer distance.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.why.1: (b) Incorrect because, before getting closer, the author could see only “something white like snow” and did not yet know whether it was a flower or a tree. The tree’s name became known only after approaching it and asking a passerby.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage only says that the author saw “something like white snow” (雪のようなもの); it does not say that the author went looking for or wanted to see real snow.
default.q.n3-27-q68-68.why.3: (d) Correct. The passage says: 「遠くに白い雪のようなものがたくさんついている木が見えました。何かと思って、①近くに行ってみると、それは桜に似た小さな花でした。」 (From a distance, I saw a tree covered with many white, snow-like things. Wondering what they were, I went closer and saw that they were small flowers resembling cherry blossoms.)
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.verdict: The correct answer is 1: Because they learned that there are cherry trees that bloom in autumn.
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.explanation:
Main point: A passerby explains that it is a type of cherry tree called “Shikizakura,” which blooms from autumn through winter. The author is very surprised because they had always thought cherry blossoms bloomed only in spring.

Question translation: The phrase “I was very surprised” appears in the passage. Why was the author surprised?
Answer choices:
1. Because they learned that there are cherry trees that bloom in autumn.
2. Because they learned that cherry blossoms come in many different colors.
3. Because they learned that cherry blossoms bloom only in spring.
4. Because the passerby knew the name of that type of cherry tree.
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「通りかかった人に『何の木ですか』と聞くと、『桜ですよ。『四季桜』といって、秋から冬に咲くのです。』と教えてくれました。桜は春にだけ咲くと思っていたので、②とてもびっくりしました。」 (The author had thought that cherry blossoms bloomed only in spring, so was very surprised to learn that there is a variety that blooms from autumn through winter.)
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.why.1: (b) Incorrect because the author's surprise concerns when the flowers bloom (in autumn and winter), not the fact that cherry blossoms come in many colors.
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.why.2: (c) Incorrect because “cherry blossoms bloom only in spring” was the author's preexisting belief (桜は春にだけ咲くと思っていた), not a new discovery that surprised the author.
default.q.n3-27-q69-69.why.3: (d) Incorrect because what surprised the author was the existence of cherry blossoms that bloom in autumn, not the fact that passersby knew the name of the flower.
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.verdict: The correct answer is 1: You only have to pay for coffee and also get toast, an egg, and salad.
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.explanation:
Summary of the main point: At a café in Nagoya, a staff member explains that the "Morning Service" means that if you order coffee or tea before 11 a.m., you receive toast, an egg, and salad for free. The author was hungry at the time, so they were very happy to receive this offer.

Question translation: The phrase "I was very happy" appears. What made the author happy?
Answer choices:
1. Being able to eat toast... while paying only for coffee.
2. Understanding what the "Morning Service" is.
3. The fact that the "Morning Service" originated in Nagoya.
4. Getting free coffee when ordering toast.
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「朝11時までにコーヒーか紅茶を頼むと、 無料でトーストと卵とサラダがつくんです。」 and 「おなかがすいていたので、③とてもうれしかったです。」 (If you order coffee or tea before 11 a.m., toast, an egg, and salad are included free of charge; because the speaker was hungry, they were very happy to receive the extra food for the price of the coffee or tea.)
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.why.1: (b) Incorrect because understanding the concept of “Morning Service” is merely additional information. The actual reason the author was happy while hungry was receiving free food together with a drink.
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the fact that this service originated in Nagoya is merely supplementary information about its origin, not the reason the author was happy.
default.q.n3-27-q70-70.why.3: (d) Incorrect because ordering coffee comes with free toast, eggs, and salad. It is a drink that comes with free food, not toast that comes with free coffee.
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.verdict: The correct answer is 1: It feels interesting because there still seem to be many new things left to discover.
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.explanation:
Main idea: Although the author has lived in Japan for two years and thought she already knew a lot, she realizes that there is still much she does not know and expresses excitement about the new experiences ahead.

Question translation: How does the writer feel about life in Japan?
Answer choices:
1. She finds it interesting because there still seem to be many things to discover.
2. She feels uneasy because quite a few things startle and surprise her.
3. She feels happy because there are similarities to her own country.
4. She finds it difficult to live there because there are too many things she does not understand.
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.why.0: (a) Correct. The passage states: 「日本についていろいろを知っていると思っていましたが、まだ知らないことがけっこうあります。」 and 「これからまたどんな経験ができるか、とても楽しみです。」 (The author realizes that there is still quite a lot they do not know about Japan and looks forward to seeing what experiences await, expressing enthusiasm and interest.)
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.why.1: (b) Incorrect. Although there were some surprises, the author felt very expectant and excited (とても楽しみ), not uneasy or restless (落ち着かない).
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.why.2: (c) Incorrect because the passage does not mention or compare the author's hometown at all.
default.q.n3-27-q71-71.why.3: (d) Incorrect because the writer has a positive attitude and eagerly welcomes the unknown; the writer does not think that having many unknown things makes life difficult (生活しにくい).

default.q.n3-27-q1-1.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (あせ): The kanji 「汗」 is read with the kun-reading 「あせ」 and means “sweat.”
default.q.n3-27-q1-1.explanation:
Meaning: I sweated while playing sports, so I took a shower.
- Sino-Japanese roots: 汗 (sweat).
- Example: 暑い日にはたくさん汗をかきます。(I sweat a lot on hot days.)
default.q.n3-27-q1-1.why.0: (a) Correct:「汗」is read「あせ」(sweat), forming the expression「汗をかく」(to sweat).
default.q.n3-27-q1-1.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「ごみ」(garbage, dust) is usually written in hiragana or with the kanji「塵」「芥」, not as a reading of「汗」.
default.q.n3-27-q1-1.why.2: (c) Incorrect: 「よごれ」 (stain) is a noun derived from 「汚れる」 (using the kanji 「汚」), not 「汗」.
default.q.n3-27-q1-1.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「なみだ」 (tears) is the reading of 「涙」, not 「汗」.
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.verdict: The correct answer is 4 (くばって): the kanji 「配」in the verb 「配る」has the kun-reading 「くばる」, whose te-form is 「くばって」.
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.explanation:
Meaning: Please distribute this notice to everyone.
- Sino-Japanese roots: 配 (to distribute, hand out).
- Example: 先生は教室でプリントを配りました。(The teacher handed out printed materials in the classroom.)
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.why.0: (a) Incorrect:「だまって」is the te-form of the verb「黙る」(だまる: to remain silent; the kanji is「黙」).
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「もらって」 is the te-form of the verb 「貰う/もらう」 (to receive).
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.why.2: (c) Incorrect:「はらって」is the te-form of the verb「払う」(はらう — to pay, brush off; kanji「払」), not the intended reading.
default.q.n3-27-q2-2.why.3: (d) Correct. 「配って」 is the te-form of 「配る」 (くばる: to distribute or share), and it fits the meaning and grammar of the sentence.
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.verdict: The correct answer is 1 (かんせい): the kanji 「完成」 has the correct on-reading 「かんせい」.
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.explanation:
Meaning: I hear that the new road is almost finished.
- 完成: completion, to complete fully.
- Example: このビルは来月完成する予定です。(This building is scheduled to be completed next month.)
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.why.0: (a) Correct: 「完成」combines 「完」(かん) and 「成」(せい), and is pronounced 「かんせい」, meaning “completion.”
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.why.1: (b) Incorrect:「けんせつ」(construction) is the reading of「建設」, not「完成」.
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.why.2: (c) Incorrect: 「かんぜん」 (complete, entirely) is the reading of 「完全」.
default.q.n3-27-q3-3.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「けんちく」(architecture; construction) is the reading of 「建築」.
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.verdict: The correct answer is 3 (しま): The kanji 「島」 has the kun-reading 「しま」, meaning “island.”
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.explanation:
Meaning: You can see many islands from here.
- 島: island.
- Example: 夏休みに南の島へ旅行に行きました。(I traveled to a southern island during summer vacation.)
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「ほし」 (star) is the reading of the kanji 「星」 (Tinh).
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.why.1: (b) Incorrect: 「とり」 (bird) is the reading of the kanji 「鳥」 (TORI in Sino-Japanese reading terminology); note that 鳥 has an additional inner stroke compared with 島.
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.why.2: (c) Correct: 「島」has the kun-reading「しま」(island; the kanji consists of the 山 radical placed above a simplified form of 鳥).
default.q.n3-27-q4-4.why.3: (d) Incorrect: 「うま」(horse) is the reading of the kanji 「馬」.
default.q.n3-27-q5-5.verdict: The correct answer is 2 (こまって): the kanji 「困」in the verb 「困る」has the kun-reading 「こまる」, whose te-form is 「こまって」.
default.q.n3-27-q5-5.explanation:
Meaning: Mr./Ms. Tanaka seems to be having some trouble.
- Kanji note: 困 (difficulty, distress, confusion).
- Example: 道が分からなくて困っています。(I am in trouble because I do not know the way.)
default.q.n3-27-q5-5.why.0: (a) Incorrect: 「まよって」is the te-form of the verb 「迷う」(まよう – to hesitate, to get lost; kanji 「迷」).
default.q.n3-27-q5-5.why.1: (b) Correct:「困って」is the te-form of「困る」(こまる — to have difficulty, be困惑ed); the kanji「困」means difficulty or distress.
